div.p: The schedulability analysis problem for many realistic task models is known to be hard (NP or coNP). As this severely restricts the application of these task models, recently there has been a considerable amount of interest in relaxed or approximate notions of schedulability, with the hope that they can be checked more efficiently.

In this paper we introduce yet another natural notion of relaxed schedulability, which is parameterized in terms of the number of paths in a task set. In the model we consider, each task is represented by a directed acyclic graph where the nodes of such a graph are annotated with execution times and deadlines. Our proposed notion of schedulability allows a certain number of paths from each task graph to be non-schedulable. For describing the relaxed schedulability analysis, we formally define a measure called pseudo-K-schedulability, which corresponds to the situation when the task set has exactly K schedulable paths. At one extreme is the classical notion of schedulability analysis, where the problem is NP hard in our and many other task models. At the other extreme of this spectrum we have the trivial notion of schedulability analysis, where no path needs to be schedulable. Problems in between allow for a flexible notion of schedulability. This paper studies the relaxed schedulability because not all paths in a code are executed. This paper shows a fundamental result, namely the membership of the pseudoschedulability problem to the class of #P-hard problems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: There have been efforts to model real-time systems, to answer scheduling-theoretic questions and to describe efficient (approximation) scheduling algorithms for these models. All models are based on an abstract framework in which a real-time system is modeled as a set of independent tasks. Each task generates a sequence of jobs, each of which is characterized by a ready-time, an execution requirement, and a deadline. Hard real-time systems required that for each job generated by a task, an amount of processor time equal to the job's execution requirement be assigned to it between its ready-time and its deadline. The traditional feasibility analysis of such a hard real-time task set is concerned with determining whether it is possible to schedule all the jobs generated by the tasks, such that they meet their deadlines under all possible choices. For the recurring real-time task model [1,2], the feasibility analysis problem is NP-hard, both for dynamic and static priorities [3]. Under these circumstances, current research in the real-time systems area has focused on obtaining efficient pseudo-polynomial algorithms for these models, or on finding polynomial time algorithms for special cases of these models, or on providing approximate schedulability.

Recently there has been a considerable amount of interest in relaxed or approximate notions of schedulability, with the hope that they can be checked more efficiently. One obvious notion of approximate schedulability is when the algorithm returns SCHEDULABLE even when a task set is not schedulable. But it is guaranteed that in such cases, no job misses its deadline by more than a prespecified error parameter. Several recently proposed algorithms for schedulability analysis with this (and other) relaxed conditions run in polynomial time and the runtime is dependent on the input error parameter.

A recent approach based on the event stream model was described in [5]. An approximation algorithm for the feasibility test of the sporadic and the generalized multiframe task system scheduled by earliest deadline first was presented. That approximation algorithm has polynomial complexity to solve the problem of schedulability analysis. As mentioned in [5], current feasibility tests for the static-priority scheduling of periodic task systems run in pseudo-polynomial time. A polynomial-time approximation scheme for feasibility in static-priority systems with arbitrary relative deadlines was described in [5], too.

Our contribution. In the context of most real-time embedded systems, each real-time task is required to model an event-driven block of code, parts of which are triggered by external events and require to be executed within a given deadline from the triggering time. Let us consider the following example with two tasks:
div.formula: Task T 1 : if (C 1 ) then execute code block B 1,1 else execute code block B 1,2 endif Task T 2 : if (C 2 ) then execute code block B 2,1 else execute code block B 2,2 endif
div.p: When doing the traditional feasibility analysis for the above task set {T 1 ,T 2 }, all possible jobs should be checked for schedulability, namely B 1,1 with B 2,1 ; B 1,1 with B 2,2 ; B 1,2 with B 2,1 ; and B 1,2 with B 2,2 . It is natural to expect that conditions C 1 and C 2 may depend on some common external events, or their evaluation may depend on some common variables. This implies that the evaluation of C 1 could be related to the evaluation of C 2 , so they will not take all the possible pairs of values from the set {false, true}. Therefore, when doing the feasibility analysis, it may not be needed to really take into consideration all the possible circumstances.

Not all paths in a program are executed with equal frequency. Hence, it is natural to consider notions of approximate schedulability which ignores certain (less frequently executed) paths. There has been a considerable amount of research in the programming languages community on using program path profiles for program debugging [6][7][8]. Our work in this paper follows this line of research. Although here we only count the number of paths and do not distinguish between different paths, we believe that this is the first step towards a more refined notion of schedulability analysis, where the distinction between less and more frequency executed paths will be made.

In this paper we introduce a new notion of "relaxed schedulability", formally called pseudoschedulability, which is parameterized in terms of the number of paths in a task set. In the model we consider, each task is represented by a directed acyclic graph where the nodes of such a graph are annotated with execution times and deadlines. Our proposed notion of schedulability allows a certain number of paths from each task graph to be non-schedulable. Intuitively, we say that a task set is schedulable even if there exists a certain combination of paths from each task graph which is not schedulable. However, in contrast to intuitive expectations, schedulability analysis for this relaxed model turns out to be more complex (#P-hard). When defining a new notion of schedulability, it is important from the theoretical and practical perspectives to establish its complexity class. Therefore, we present here a major fundamental complexity result about the pseudo-schedulability problem, namely its membership to the class of #Phard problems.

The model. A task modeling a block of code on a single processor platform can be represented by a directed acyclic graph (denoted as dag) with a unique source and a unique sink vertex. Associated with each vertex v is its execution requirement e(v), where e(v) > 0, which can be determined at compile time, and deadline d(v), where d(v) > 0. Except the source vertex, all the other vertices have in-arcs (i.e., arcs pointing to themselves), and except the sink vertex, all the vertices have out-arcs (i.e., arcs pointing from themselves). Given an arbitrary vertex v, the set of vertices {v 1 , ..., v m } having in-arcs to v is called the set of direct-in descendants of v. Similarly, the set of vertices {v 1 , ..., v n } having out-arcs from v is called the set of direct-out descendants of v. If the vertices v 1 , v 2 , ..., v n are linked by the directed arcs (v 1 ,v 2 ), (v 2 ,v 3 ), ..., (v n-1 ,v n ), the sequence (v 1 , ..., v n ) is called a path. By maximal path, we mean a path from the source to the sink vertex. Without loss of generality, we may suppose that all the paths in the dag are terminating eventually in the sink vertex. This is not a restriction as we can consider a new dummy sink vertex which has in-arcs from other vertices. So, we shall suppose that for each vertex v of a task graph, there exists a path from the source to v and another path from v to the sink vertex. Whenever the vertex v is triggered, the code corresponding to it has to be executed (which takes e(v) amount of time) within the next d(v) time units.

The semantics of the execution of such a task graph state that the source vertex can be triggered at any time, and once a vertex v is triggered then the next vertex v' can be triggered only if there exists a directed edge (v, v'). If there exist directed edges (v, v') and (v, v'') from the vertex v then only one among v' and v'' can be triggered, after the triggering of v. In general, a path (v 1 , v 2 , ..., v k ), getting triggered at time instants t 1 ,t 2 , ..., t k is legal if and only if there exist directed edges (v i ,v i+1 ) and the code corresponding to vertex v i is executed within the time interval (t i ,t i + d(v i )], for all i ∈ {1, ..., k-1}. The feasibility analysis for a task set. A task set T = {T 1 ,T 2 , ..., T k } consists of a collection of dags, the vertices of which can get triggered independently of each other. A legal triggering sequence for T is obtained by merging together (ordered by triggered times) the legal triggering sequences of the constituting tasks. In order to introduce a more relaxed view on classical schedulability, we denote by #P i the total number of distinct maximal paths in T i . We say that the task set T is pseudo-Kschedulable, where K is a positive integer, if and only if there exist K legal triggering paths for T. The case K = 0 is a very special one. We say that T is pseudo-0-schedulable if there is no legal triggering for T. In this case, T may be also called an inherent nonschedulable task set.
Given T such a pseudo-K-schedulable task set, K ≥1, we distinguish three important cases, depending on K:

(i) T is pseudo-#P-schedulable if and only if K is the product of #P 1 , ..., and #P k . In this case, the pseudo-K-schedulability matches exactly the traditional definition of schedulability. In other words, T is pseudo-#P -schedulable if and only if all possible paths in T are legal triggering paths;

(ii) T is pseudo-1-schedulable if and only if K is 1. In this case, the pseudo-K-schedulability represents the most relaxed version of schedulability. In other words, T is pseudo-1-schedulable if and only if there exists (at least) one combination of paths from T i which constitute a legal triggering path for T;
(iii) The complementary situation of the above two cases is when 1<X< #P.

The motivation of considering the latter two cases is because in practice, some paths may have smaller chances to get triggered than others. In this case, the pseudo-K-schedulability will consider only the most probable triggered paths of every task graph T i.

Another important motivation to consider pseudo-K-schedulability, where 1 ≤ X < #P, against traditional schedulability (i.e., pseudo-#Pschedulability) is because of the efficiency of schedulability analysis. Obviously, for deciding whether a task set T is pseudo-#P -schedulable, it is necessary to visit all the nodes of the task set. This leads to an exponential time complexity. On the contrary, when checking for pseudo-K-schedulability, where K is not necessarily #P, it might be possible to visit only a few sub-graphs of the task set. For example, it is expected that the execution time for deciding pseudo-1-schedulability would be less than the execution time for deciding pseudo-#Pschedulability. So, when doing schedulability analysis, it is likely to analyse first the pseudo-1schedulability (as the most relaxed condition for feasibility analysis). Let us consider a path P =(v 1 , ..., v n ), where v 1 , ..., v n are vertices labelled with (e(v 1 ),d(v 1 )), ..., (e(v n ),d(v n )). Of course, we suppose that e(v i ) ≤ d(v i ), ∀i ∈{1, ..., n}. We denote by ET(P) the execution time of path P as e(v 1 )+ ... +e(v n ) and by D(P) the deadline of path P as d(v 1 )+ ... +d(v n ).

The Pseudo-K-Schedulability problem: We define formally now the general computation problem as a counting version for pseudo-Kschedulability decision problem:
div.formula: Input: A task set T= {T 1 ,T 2 , ..., T k }, k ≥ 1 Output: Number of legal triggering sequences of T.
div.p: One of the utility of the pseudo-K-schedulability problem is to define a measure, K, which corresponds to the case when the task set has exactly K schedulable sequences. As such, we provide insights into the boundary between "not at all" schedulable (that is, K =0) and "completely" schedulable (K is the maximum number of distinct paths). Our paper deals with a more general scheduling analysis problem. When considering new problems, it is likely that the most important issue is to identify to which complexity class that problem belongs. When considering intractable problems, the first expectation is to check if the given problem is NP-hard. One way to prove this membership is to reduce the given problem to a well-known NP-complete problem. The first discovered NP-complete problem was the (SAT) problem [9]: "Given a propositional formula F, does it have at least a truth assignment?" Unfortunately, the (SAT) problem is not enough powerful to simulate the pseudo-K-schedulability problem. In the following, we shall show how can we reduced our pseudo-schedulability problem to a counting problem. A counting problem P determines how many solutions exist, not just an answer "Yes/No" like a decision problem. A counting problem P is in #P if there is a non-deterministic algorithm such that for each instance I the number of guesses that lead to the acceptance of I is exactly the number of distinct solutions of P regarding I and such that the length of the longest accepting computation is bounded by a polynomial in the length of I [10]. The problem of counting the number of truth assignments (denoted by #SAT) was proved to be #P -complete [10]. Given F a propositional formula over the set of variables V, we denote by det V (F) the number of truth assignments of F (also called the determinant of F over V , [11]). Formally, the (#SAT) problem is:
div.formula: Input: A propositional formula F over set of variables V Output: det V (F )
div.p: The structure of the paper is as follows: Section 2 presents a criteria to check if a task set is schedulable; Section 3 describes an algorithm for converting the pseudo-K-schedulability problem to the (#SAT) problem; Related and future works conclude this paper.

div.head: Preliminary results
div.p: This section is devoted to theoretical results regarding the schedulability of our model. The next lemma shows a necessary and suficient condition for scheduling a task set having two tasks only. Lemma 2.1 Let P 1 =(v 1 , ..., v n ) and P 2 =(v ' 1 , ..., v' m ) be two arbitrary paths in the task graph T= {T 1 ,T 2 }, where n, m ≥1. Then P 1 and P 2 can be triggered independently if and only if ∀ P' 1 , P' 2 subpaths of P 1 , P 2 , we have ET (P' 1 ) +ET (P' 2 ) ≤max{D(P' 1 ),D(P' 2 )}.
Proof Both implications can be proved by induction on the number of vertices of paths P 1 and P 2 , that is, n + m. For simplicity, we prove only the ( ) implication.

Induction Basis: Let us take n=m=1. Suppose that the vertices v1 and v' 1 are labelled with (e(v 1 ), d(v 1 )), and (e(v' 1 ), d(v' 1 )), respectively. Obviously, there exist the legal triggering sequences v 1 , v' 1 or v' 1 , v 1 if and only if e(v 1 )+ e(v' 1 ) ≤ d(v 1 ) or e(v 1 )+ e(v' 1 ) ≤ d(v' 1 ). The latter conditions are equivalent to e(v 1 ) + e(v' 1 ) ≤ max{d(v 1 ),d(v' 1 )}, which represent Lemma 2.1's conclusion.

div.head: Induction
div.p: Step: Let us denote by p 1 and p 2 the number of vertices of two sub-paths of P 1 and P 2 . We know from the inductive hypothesis that the implication holds for all p 1 and p 2 such that 1≤ p 1 ≤ n, 1≤ p 2 ≤ m. We have to prove that the implication holds for all p' 1 and p' 2 such that 1≤ p' 1 ≤n, 1≤ p' 2 ≤m, and p' 1 + p' 2 = p 1 + p 2 +1. Without loss of generality, we suppose that p' 1 = p 1 +1 and p' 2 = p 2 . Denoting the sub-paths of P 1 and P 2 having p 1 and p 2 vertices as P' 1 and P' 2 , we consider the new sub-path P" 1 as the sequence between P' 1 and a new vertex, say v, labeled with (e(v),d(v)), where e(v) ≤ d(v). Obviously, the sub-path from P 2 remains unchanged, namely P" 2 = P' 2. According to definitions of ET and D, we get: ET(P" 1 )= ET(P' 1 )+ e and D(P" 1 )= D(P' 1 )+ d.

Knowing that there exists a legal triggering of P" 1 and P" 2 , it follows that there exists a legal triggering for P' 1 and P' 2 . According to the induction hypothesis, we get ET(P' 1 ) + ET(P' 2 ) ≤ max{D(P' 1 ), D(P' 2 )}. We distinguish two cases:
(i) ET (P' 1 ) + ET(P' 2 ) ≤ D(P' 1 ). Since e(v) ≤ d(v), it follows that ET(P" 1 ) + ET(P" 2 ) ≤ D(P" 1 ), which implies what we needed to prove: ET(P" 1 ) + ET(P" 2 ) ≤ max{D(P" 1 ), D(P" 2 )}.

ii) Otherwise, we have ET (P' 1 ) + ET (P' 2 ) ≤ D(P' 2 ). Since ET (P' 1 ) + ET (P' 2 ) > D(P' 1 ), it follows that the last executed job was from P' 2 , and not from P' 1 . Knowing that there exists a legal triggering for P" 1 and P" 2 , it results that the difference between the deadline of v and the execution time of v is bigger than the difference of execution times of P' 1 , P' 2 and the deadline of P' 1 . Formally, this may be expressed as d(v) -e(v) ≥ ET(P' 1 ) + ET(P' 2 ) -D(P' 1 ). Thus, this is equivalent with ET(P" 1 ) + ET(P" 2 ) ≤ D(P" 1 ), which leads to our conclusion. ■ Lemma 2.1 may be easily generalized as a scheduling result for k tasks.

Theorem 2.1 Let T = {T 1 , ..., T k } be a task set and P 1 , ..., P k be arbitrary paths of T 1 , ..., T k , respectively. Then P 1 , ..., P k can be triggered independently if and only if ∀ P' 1 , ..., P' k sub-paths of P 1 , ..., P k , we have ET (P' 1 )+ ... + ET (P' k ) ≤ max{D(P' 1 ), ..., D(P' k )}.

This means that it ensures to prove Lemma 3.1 only for k =1. We shall proceed by induction on the number of paths in T 1 . The induction basis is obvious, since for only one single path, there are no branches in T 1 . Therefore all propositional variables are evaluated to true, which implies that the determinant is 1.

Let us now assume that we add to T 1 one new path. We denote the resulted task graph by T' 1 . This means that some m new arcs and m -1 new vertices namely when code blocks run in an infinite loop. Particular models are sporadic [12], multiframe [13], generalized multiframe [14] and recurring branching [1]. For the ease of the presentation, the model we considered here is slightly simpler than that of [2,3] in the sense that we do not consider neither the recurring behaviour of the task graphs nor the intertriggering separation time between two distinct vertices. Since we are primarily concerned about complexity analysis, modelling recurring executions is not really necessary. Moreover, as we proved that non-recurring model turns out to be #P -complete, the recurring model seems to be at least as hard as the former one.

There were efforts which described approaches for the specification and analysis of scheduling problems of real-time systems. One such example was based on algebra of communicating shared resources with value-passing (ACSR-VP), which is an extension of a real-time process algebra, with value-passing capabilities and parameterized processes [15]. ACSR-VP was used to describe an instance of a scheduling problem as a process that has parameters of the problem as free variables. The specification is analyzed by means of a symbolic algorithm, and a boolean expression with free variables is produced as an outcome of the analysis. The solution to a boolean expression identifies under what values of the unknown parameters the system becomes schedulable.

div.head: Conclusions and future work
div.p: We proposed a new notion of schedulability, which allows a certain number of paths from each task graph to be non-schedulable. For describing the relaxed schedulability analysis, we formally define a measure called pseudo-K-schedulability, which corresponds to the situation when the task set has exactly K schedulable paths. In this way, we provide insights into the boundary between "not at all" schedulable and "completely" schedulable. Although we might expect that the schedulability analysis for this relaxed model to be simpler, this does not hold. In fact, the pseudo-schedulability problem belongs to a larger complexity class than NP -complete, namely #P-complete. This implies that the pseudoschedulability analysis is harder to be solved. Even so, it offers the "full" picture of how schedulable a task set can be.

As future work, it is possible to look for complexity results of the pseudo-schedulability problem for other models. Even if we showed the #Pcompleteness of the pseudoschedulability problem only for the non-recurring model, it is expected that the pseudo-schedulability problem for the recurring model to be at least as hard as #P class of problems.

The other implication is similar, so we conclude the lemma. ■ Theorem 3.1 is the correctness result for Algorithm (SchSat), which proves that the pseudoschedulability problem can be reduced to the (#SAT) problem. Theorem 3.1 Let T = {T 1 , ..., T k }be a task set and F be the propositional formula over V provided by Algorithm (SchSat) as output. Then T is pseudo-Kschedulable if and only if det V (F) = X. Proof We proceed by reverse induction on K. The induction basis, namely the case when K = #P, has been proven in Lemma 3.1. Let us prove now the induction step. Knowing that T is pseudo-mschedulable iff det V (F) = m, we have to prove that T is pseudo-(m -1)-schedulable iff det V (F) = m-1, where 0 <m ≤ #P .

We prove only the ( ) implication, as the other implication can be done similarly. Let us consider T = {T 1 , ..., T k } a pseudo-(m-1)-schedulable task set and F be the corresponding propositional formula over V. This means that there exist m -1 legal triggering paths for T. Obviously, it is possible to change some execution times and/or deadlines such that one nonlegal triggering path having nodes from T 1 , ..., T k becomes schedulable. This is a path built by merging maximal paths from the source vertex to the sink vertex of each T i , where i ∈{1, ..., k}. This corresponds to a inter-tasks clause like this: C new = {A (1) 1,2 ,...,┐A (1) p1-1,p1 , ….,┐A (k) 1,2 ,…,┐A (k) pk-1,pk } So, the new task set, obtained by making this path a legal triggering, will be pseudo-m-schedulable. According to the inductive hypothesis, it follows that det V (F ∪{C new })= m. But C new corresponds to a truth assignment for F, so det V (F )= m -1. ■
We have proved that the pseudo-schedulability problem is in #P.
